You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Soft and conducting organic materials are ideal candidates for stretchable bioelectronics and wearable devices. Despite recent advances, our understanding of conducting polymer nanostructures and how they arise remains incomplete, given the limited high-resolution studies and molecular-level descriptions of these systems. Here, we employ cryogenic transmission electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to investigate the evolution of poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrenesulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) morphology in solution and the resulting solid state structure in the presence of ionic and molecular additives. Our results reveal the formation of heterostructural elongated fibers consisting of PEDOT:PSS micelles in solution. Cryo-EM further reveals that additives increase the number of fibrils, in addition to inducing the formation of crystalline domains. We observe that fibril and crystalline phases in solutions act as a template for the growth of these nanostructures in the solid state. Furthermore, exploiting cryo-EM reveals the role of solid-liquid interactions in PEDOT:PSS through the imaging of PEDOT:PSS nanostructures after the hydration of thin films. Hydration leads to the swelling of heterostructural fibers while reducing the crystalline domain size. Such behavior explains the mechanical robustness of PEDOT:PSS thin films processed with various additives as well as the high electrical conductivity of PEDOT:PSS in applications such as organic electorchemical transistors.

---

## Introduction

Mixed ionic-electronic conductors have attracted tremendous attention due to their unique properties and applicability in a wider range of devices, such as batteries1, fuel cells2, and organic electrochemical transistors3,4. Organic mixed-ionic electronic conductors, particularly conjugated polymeric systems, have opened new prospects in applications in biosensing5 and neuromorphic computing6. Poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrenesulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) is one of the most widely used polymeric mixed ionic-electronic conductors due to its commercial availability, high electrical/ionic conductivity7,8, and mechanical compliance7,9. This prototypical mixed conductor relies on a mixture of conjugated and ionic polymers, although how interactions between the two components, processing, and additives govern assembly, microstructure and macroscopic properties remain an open question.

PEDOT:PSS in its pristine form possesses a low electrical conductivity, near 1 S/cm3,7,10,11. The addition of high boiling point solvents11, “secondary dopants” such as ionic liquids and salts12,13, and post-deposition acid treatment14 can substantially enhance electrical conductivity by three orders of magnitude over their pristine counterparts. In addition to the significant boost to conductivity, ionic and molecular additives have also been linked to an increase in the stretchability and flexibility of PEDOT:PSS, a key property for fabricating wearable electronics7,12,13.

A large body of work has focused on studying structure-function relationships in PEDOT:PSS under different processing conditions7,12,13,15–19. Despite these efforts, a holistic picture describing the PEDOT:PSS morphology remains elusive, in part due to morphological complexities and the lack of real space imaging techniques conveying the solution and solid-state properties. For instance, we commonly accept that PEDOT:PSS microstructure consists of core-shell micelles with PEDOT-rich cores and PSS-rich coronas. Despite this common assumption, the reported core-shell size extracted from neutron, X-ray, and light scattering techniques ranges from a few nanometers15 to hundreds of nanometers20,21. The role of additives further complicates the morphological picture3. X-ray and neutron scattering measurements point to the formation of rod-like structures21 in PEDOT:PSS with added salts, as well as an increase in the degree of crystallinity7 of PEDOT:PSS through the breakdown of core-shell and phase segregation of PEDOT and PSS. Nevertheless, important aspects of the PEDOT:PSS morphology remain unresolved, such as the size and distribution of crystalline domains and the correlation between rod-like aggregates and crystalline phases. Despite the partial success of the core-shell breakdown model, this description fails to explain multiple PEDOT:PSS properties, such as the simultaneous increase in electrical conductivity and increase in mechanical compliance, in particular of modern formulations of PEDOT:PSS7,22. This behavior is in contrast with other conjugated polymer systems, where a trade-off exists between charge transport (and crystallinity) and mechanical compliance23,24. We propose that the lack of a comprehensive morphological model predicting the physical properties of PEDOT:PSS mainly stems from reliance on scattering and spectroscopy techniques to characterize the complex global and local morphology of PEDOT:PSS.

Here, we reveal how the microstructure impacts the mechanical and electrical properties of PEDOT:PSS using a combination of cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS), and X-ray scattering. Exploiting high-resolution cryo-EM reveals the nanostructure evolution of PEDOT:PSS dispersions upon the addition of ionic and nonionic additives. We used bis(trifluoromethane)sulfonimide lithium (Li-TFSI) and 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide (EMIM-TFSI) salts due to their strong cation exchange capability with PEDOT:PSS22. Polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) was selected as a nonionic additive because it can enable highly-conductive, stretchable PEDOT:PSS-based bioelectronics9,10. Our results reveal that ionic and PEGDA additives lead to the formation of elongated fibers and chain packing in solutions. Further analysis of cryo-EM results reveals that elongated fibers form through the coalescence and self-assembly of PEDOT:PSS micelles that often exhibit an outer layer of extended and stacked chains. The presence of these heterostructural fibers has direct implications on the mechanical and electrical properties of PEDOT:PSS.

High-resolution cryo-EM imaging of solid films, which are processed from PEDOT:PSS solutions with the various additives, confirms the formation and growth of crystalline domains and heterostructural fibers in solid samples. Furthermore, by employing a combination of cryo-EM, EELS, and an automated crystal feature extraction framework (called Graph based Analysis of Transmission Electron Microscopy, GRATEv225), we show how exposure to moisture reorganizes the PEDOT:PSS nanostructure leading to smaller crystalline domains while heterostructural fibers swell. The former observation is consistent with the reduction in electrical conductivity of PEDOT:PSS in the presence of moisture26,27, while the latter explains the complex mechanical properties of PEDOT:PSS with ionic and PEGDA additives. Our results also show that additives can enhance the hydrophilicity of PEDOT:PSS, leading to higher moisture absorbance and resulting in higher mechanical compliance and a larger crack onset strain in these samples. Subsequently, the combination of heterostructural fibers swelling and reorganization of crystalline domains leads to the formation of simultaneously conductive and stretchable PEDOT:PSS thin films. Our work provides a framework for the complex interplay between morphological, mechanical, and electrical properties of modern formulations of PEDOT:PSS used in different applications, such as implant electrodes5, wearable electronics9, and organic electrochemical transistors8,28.

---

## Results

Cryo-EM of PEDOT:PSS dispersions
Beam damage is one of the main factors limiting the resolution and detailed analysis of organic structures in real space. Cryo-EM has been extensively used in the study of biological samples29,30 to both minimize electron beam damage31–33 and enable studies of hydrated (vitrified) samples31–33. We used cryo-EM to track PEDOT:PSS self-assembly with salt additives. Previously, we showed that the addition of ionic species lead to the formation and self-assembly of elongated fibers in the solution phase of PEDOT:PSS3. Other recent studies have also reported elongated fibrils in doped PEDOT:PSS17,34,35. Despite these initial observations, the lack of high-resolution structural imaging of PEDOT:PSS in either solution or solid films precludes a complete description of PEDOT:PSS phase formation and microstructure. Specifically, the distribution of crystalline domains and the inner structure of elongated fibers in highly conductive and stretchable PEDOT:PSS remain underexplored.

Solution cryo-EM measurements were performed on vitrified PEDOT:PSS samples at liquid nitrogen temperature (see the Methods section for details). Figure 1a–b shows a schematic of the plunge freezing of TEM grids and the chemical structure of PEDOT:PSS and ionic and PEGDA additives, respectively. Schematics of PEDOT:PSS dispersions containing isolated micelles and aggregated micelles in heterostructural fibers are shown in Fig. 1c–d, respectively. High-resolution cryo-EM shows the presence of two distinct domains in neat PEDOT:PSS solutions, (i) isolated micelles with a size of 4.1 ± 1.3 nm, and (ii) elongated fibers (Fig. 1e–g). On the other hand, PEDOT:PSS solutions containing ionic and PEGDA additives, in addition to the higher density of elongated fibers, also show lattice planes of PEDOT:PSS in solution (Fig. 1h–p).

Previous work has used X-ray scattering measurements to propose that PEDOT:PSS micelles consist of a PEDOT-rich nanocrystalline core and a PSS-rich corona15. The higher mass density of the crystalline PEDOT-rich core when compared to the amorphous PSS-rich corona leads us to assume that electron scattering from the micelles is dominated by the core region. As a result, we associate the ca. 3–4 nm features in cryo-EM micrographs with the PEDOT-rich core of PEDOT:PSS micelles. At this point, the size of the PSS-rich corona region cannot be independently extracted from cryo-EM, mainly due to the small scattering contrast between solvated PSS-rich regions and water.

A comparison of micelle sizes in solutions reveals that ionic additives decrease the diameter of PEDOT-rich cores (3.1 ± 0.5 nm), while solutions with PEGDA exhibit micelle sizes comparable to those of neat PEDOT:PSS (3.9 ± 0.8 nm) (see Figs. S1–S2). A reduction in micelle size upon the addition of salts to PEDOT:PSS has been previously reported, which has been attributed to the screening of interchain charge repulsion15,36. Previously reported micelle sizes extracted from solutions of PEDOT:PSS using measurements of the hydrodynamic radius obtained from dynamic light scattering (DLS) show a dominant size distribution between 3 to 15 nm and a few micelles up to 30 nm37. As shown in Fig. 1, we also observe smaller micelles and larger aggregate structures. In addition, given that solvated PSS chains are likely not visible in cryo-EM, we expect micelles in our micrographs to appear smaller than values reported from DLS or SAXS. The micelle size apparent from our cryo-EM images and previous work37 suggests that PEDOT exists as oligomers with limited chain lengths.

We attribute the chain stacking with 1.4–1.6 nm spacing, observed in solution cryo-EM micrographs, to PEDOT:PSS lamella stacks that have previously been attributed to the presence of alternating PEDOT and PSS chains3,38. Examples of these lamellae lattice fringes (parallel lines in cryo-EM micrographs) are indicated by the orange arrows in Fig. 1i–o. To rule out Fresnel-fringe or defocus artifacts, we measured the lamellar spacing at multiple defocus settings; the spacing (~1.5 nm) remained invariant with defocus (Figs. S3–S4). As mentioned before, cryo-EM micrographs reveal fibers with a complex heterostructure of coalesced polymer micelles and extended stacked chains that we attribute to a crystalline, or “proto-crystalline” phase. Figure 1h–j shows that these heterostructural fibers consist of small micelles (core of about 3 nm) surrounded by a crystalline phase parallel to the long axis of the fibers.

As shown in Fig. S5, and consistent with the Vitrobot-prepared (“blot-based”) micrographs in Fig. 1, samples prepared with Vitroject (non-contact, jet-based)39 also display clear elongated fibers in PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI dispersions. The agreement between blot-based and non-contact preparation highlights that these fibers are intrinsic to the PEDOT:PSS formulations, not artifacts of the blotting process. Furthermore, these heterostructural fibers can also be observed in PEDOT:PSS+EMIM-TFSI and PEDOT:PSS+PEGDA solution mixtures (Fig. 1k–m, n–p). Additional examples of micrographs collected at different defocus settings and micrographs highlighting lamella stacks plus micelles in PEDOT:PSS dispersions are shown in Figs. S6 and S7. We observe that increasing the self-assembly time after adding the additives leads to more elongated fibers and fewer isolated micelles in PEDOT:PSS+EMIM-TFSI dispersions (Fig. S8). This rise in fiber density with time, together with the drop in isolated micelles, is consistent with our prior results3 and points to micelle coalescence driving the formation of elongated fibers. As will be discussed in the following sections, the presence of crystalline phases and heterostructural fibers has a significant effect on the physical and electrical properties of PEDOT:PSS thin films.

Given the similar trends across various PEDOT:PSS systems, subsequent sections center on PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI as a model system to examine morphological evolution of PEDOT:PSS processed with additives.

Cryo-EM of solid films
To elucidate how films assemble from PEDOT:PSS solutions, we performed cryo-EM on spin-coated thin films of PEDOT:PSS processed with and without additives. At lower magnifications, neat PEDOT:PSS films (Fig. S9) show a uniform morphology, while magnified micrographs also show the presence of both PEDOT:PSS lamella stacks and micelles. The crystalline domains in neat PEDOT:PSS are generally around 10-15 nm long and <5 nm wide. The PEDOT-rich cores of the micelles in neat PEDOT:PSS films have an oval shape with a long axis of ~3.5 nm. Unlike in neat PEDOT:PSS solutions, elongated fibers are not visible in cryo-EM micrographs of solid PEDOT:PSS films. We speculate that fibers in neat PEDOT:PSS strongly coalesce or breakdown, making them challenging to identify in micrographs. On the other hand, PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI (see Fig. 2a) and PEDOT:PSS+PEGDA (see Fig. S10) samples show a significantly more heterogeneous structure than neat PEDOT:PSS. This is in line with the presence of more fibers and crystalline domains in solutions of additive-containing PEDOT:PSS formulations. Similarly to the aggregates visible in solution, high magnification of the structure reveals that elongated fibers in PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films appear to form through the coalescence of polymer micelles (Fig. 2b). Indeed, lamellar structures are now apparent throughout the film and are not limited to areas surrounding micellar fibers.

Overall, we see a close resemblance between solution and solid domains in PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI, with larger crystalline domains (>20 nm thick crystals) observed in the solid samples. Thus, the heterostructural fibers and crystalline domains in solution template the growth of the subsequent structures in solid thin films. We also see a fibril structure in samples containing ethylene glycol as a solvent additive and (3-glycidyloxypropyl)trimethoxysilane (GOPS) cross-linker (Fig. S12). PEDOT:PSS+ethylene glycol+GOPS is perhaps the most common formulation used in organic electrochemical transistor devices. Further analysis of cryo-EM micrographs using frequency cut-off filters (see Fig. S13) reveals that the crystalline domains in PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI do not align with the orientation of heterostructured fibers. Therefore, although large fibrils in PEDOT:PSS are assumed to be composed of PEDOT (or PEDOT-rich) crystals11,13,17, our work clearly shows that micelles, likely composed of PEDOT and PSS mixtures, make up these domains. We speculate that this structure, with PEDOT proto-crystals coating the outside of micellar structures, is crucial for establishing highly conducting phases by precluding the need to disrupt an insulating PSS corona that was previously assumed to be present.

Besides the PEDOT:PSS lamellar phase with 1.4–1.6 nm spacing (which could correspond to the PEDOT:PSS (100) crystal planes)40, cryo-EM also captures domains with a lattice spacing of ~0.7 nm. The latter spacing corresponds to the pure PEDOT lamella stacking (see Fig. S14 for cryo-EM micrograph and subsequent FFT of the crystalline domains with ~0.7 nm spacing). Compared to in solution, lamella stacks spacings appear to be slightly larger in solid samples. To further investigate PEDOT:PSS microstructure, we performed grazing incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) measurements on PEDOT:PSS samples with and without additives. Figures 2e and S11 show 1D GIWAXS profiles along the in-plane and out-of-plane orientations, respectively, for neat PEDOT:PSS and PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films. Figure S11 further shows GIWAXS profiles of additional PEDOT:PSS thin films processed with additives. Previous work has associated the peaks at 0.39 Å−1 (16.1 Å) and 0.28 Å−1 (22.5 Å) with stacking of two different variations of alternating PEDOT and PSS chains18,38,41 (as shown in Fig. S15 and Table S1). The peaks at 0.89 Å−1 (7.1 Å), 1.27 Å−1 (4.9 Å), and 1.8 Å−1 (3.5 Å) are associated with the neat PEDOT lamella stacking7, PSS chain stacking18, and PEDOT π-π stacking, respectively18.

The reported diffraction peak positions and spacings can vary slightly depending on the type of additive and measurement conditions, such as humidity18,42. Because lattice fringes are visible only when the electron beam is approximately parallel to those lattice planes, periodicities oriented out-of-plane, which project along the beam, are not visible in TEM micrographs. Thus, the spacings apparent in in-plane GIWAXS (lamella stacks with 15–16 Å spacing) correspond to visible chain stacking in TEM micrographs. Overall, the combination of solution and solid film cryo-EM provides an opportunity to identify key features of the microstructure and how they evolve from solution to film.

Solid-liquid Interactions
We expect different responses from crystalline domains and heterostructural fibers when exposed to moisture. To investigate this hypothesis, we exposed PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films to moisture (100% relative humidity (RH)) before plunge-freezing the samples with liquid ethane (see Methods section for further details). This approach allows us to monitor the morphological evolution in high-conductivity PEDOT:PSS thin films in the presence of water.

As shown in cryo-EM images in Fig. 2c, upon exposure to moisture, PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films show a uniform morphology with some inhomogeneity observed in the density of PEDOT:PSS micelles. We also show HRTEM images of PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI recorded at 30% and 100% relative humidity under varying defocus conditions in Fig. S16. Moisture exposure improves the contrast of polymer micelles, as can be seen in Fig. 2d. Given the expected thickness increase of PEDOT:PSS films upon hydration42,43, the improvement in scattering contrast cannot be explained by reduced inelastic electron scattering or a reduced number of overlapping features in hydrated samples. Subsequently, we deduce that upon exposure to moisture, the PSS-rich shell of the micelles swells, decreasing the scattering from the shell and improving the contrast between the PEDOT-rich core and the swollen PSS-rich corona. This shows that heterostructural fibers consist of self-assembled core-shell PEDOT:PSS micelles that swell upon exposure to water. Figure 2f shows the 1D small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) SAXS profiles of drop cast neat PEDOT:PSS and PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI at two different RH levels. While the SAXS profiles from neat PEDOT:PSS show minimal differences between 40% and 85% RH, PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI samples show a clear change that corresponds to the formation of mesoscale structures upon exposure to higher moisture.

The limited field of view of high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) images often limits analyses to qualitative changes. Automated sampling and large-quantity data collection, developed for the study of biological samples44–47, may promote the extraction of quantitative microstructural information from HRTEM. This approach remains under-explored for the quantitative analysis of the morphology of conjugated polymers. Recently, Gamdha et al.25 developed software for a Graph based Analysis of Transmission Electron Microscopy (GRATEv2) of polymeric samples25,48, which can identify crystalline domains from images at high speed, providing information on domain size, orientation, and area.

We employed GRATEv2 to analyze crystalline domain size and distribution in PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films before and after hydration (exposure to 100% RH). HRTEM micrographs of PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films at 30% and 100% RH can be seen in Fig. 3a–b, respectively. Figure 3c shows the flow chart of the GRATEv2 analysis. Figure 3d–e shows the subsequent GRATEv2 output figures of micrographs presented in Fig. 3a–b, respectively. The crystalline domains with a lattice spacing of ~1.5-16 nm ((100) PEDOT:PSS lamella spacing) are shown with the purple regions. Additional cryo-EM examples at 30% and 100% RH, together with their GRATEv2 analyses, are shown in Figure S17. A histogram of crystalline domain sizes is presented in Fig. 3f. HRTEM shows that hydration leads to the formation of smaller crystalline domains in PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI with an average domain area of 117 nm2 at 30% RH versus 74 nm2 at 100% RH. These results show that crystalline domains respond differently to water absorption compared to heterostructural fibers. While crystalline domains shrink in size, heterostructural fibers swell significantly upon hydration. The distinct difference in microstructural evolution of crystalline domains and heterostructural fibers upon hydration shows that these two domains possess different nanostructures. As will be discussed in the next section, the direct imaging of nanocrystalline domains and heterostructural fibers allows us to explain the mechanical and electrical properties of PEDOT:PSS upon exposure to humidity and moisture.

Electrical and mechanical properties of PEDOT:PSS
The high electrical conductivity and mechanical compliance of PEDOT:PSS, often achieved by the addition of ionic additives, are the main factors driving the widespread use of this mixed ionic-electronic polymer in various applications3,7,9,49. In this section, we explore the correlation between morphology, conductivity, and mechanical properties of PEDOT:PSS in the presence of ionic additives. Consistent with prior studies7,12,13,22, we observe an increase in the electrical conductivity of PEDOT:PSS thin films by two to three orders of magnitude following film processing using ionic additives and water treatment of salt-containing films (Fig. S18). The significant increase in electrical conductivity of PEDOT:PSS is often closely correlated with an increase in crystallinity of PEDOT:PSS processed with different additives7,12,13. This is consistent with the larger number of crystalline domains observed in cryo-EM of PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films (See Fig. 3d).

Compared to the mechanisms behind the enhancement of electrical conductivity, the improvement in mechanical properties of PEDOT:PSS in the presence of ionic additives is less understood. To ascertain the role of structure on mechanical properties in PEDOT:PSS, we performed crack onset strain (COS) measurements of neat PEDOT:PSS and PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI at two different humidity levels (See Methods section for more details). At 70% RH, cracks appear in neat PEDOT:PSS and PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI at 11±5 % and 27±8 % strains, respectively (see Fig. 4a). On the other hand, when the same measurements were performed in a 0% RH glovebox, both neat PEDOT:PSS and the additive-loaded samples cracked at much lower strains (~2% COS), with dry PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI showing even slightly less stretchability compared to neat PEDOT:PSS. Upon hydration, a similar increasing trend in COS is also observed in PEDOT:PSS+PEGDA (Fig. S19). These results indicate that moisture uptake plays a substantial role in the mechanical properties of PEDOT:PSS processed with additives, including salts50.

To further investigate the effect of ionic additives and their subsequent removal upon water treatment, we performed thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) on neat PEDOT:PSS and PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI; results are shown in Fig. 4b. Neat PEDOT:PSS show two main mass loss transitions: the first transition completes around 100 °C; this transition is due to the evaporation of moisture within the PEDOT:PSS structure. The second transition at ~275 °C is associated with the chemical degradation of PEDOT:PSS. On the other hand, PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI shows a significantly different TGA profile. TGA from PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI does not show clear thermal transitions, but instead a continuous loss of sample mass, with an overall larger mass loss percentage compared to neat PEDOT:PSS. After water treatment (removing added salts), the thermogram reverts to the two-step profile for neat PEDOT:PSS, confirming that water absorption due to Li-TFSI is responsible for the broadened, continuous loss of sample mass (Fig. S20). The water uptake of films containing Li-TFSI likely leads to the formation of water-salt complexes within the PEDOT:PSS structure51,52.

We also measured the water uptake due to Li-TFSI using scanning transmission electron microscopy-electron energy loss spectroscopy (STEM-EELS) at room temperature and cryogenic conditions (Fig. S21). STEM-EELS allows us to establish a compositional-morphological relationship in PEDOT:PSS thin films processed with hydrophilic additives. Although ionic additives are linked to the improved stretchability of PEDOT:PSS, upon water treatment, the stretchability of PEDOT:PSS films significantly drops due to the removal of these additives13. We associate this behavior with the formation of water-salt complexes in PEDOT:PSS and subsequent elimination of these complexes after water treatment. This is consistent with the increase in oxygen composition (as an indicator for water absorption) when we compare PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films before and after salt removal (Fig. 4c and Fig. S22).

---

## Methods

Solution preparation
PEDOT:PSS solutions were purchased from Heraeus (Clevios PH1000) and were used without further modification for neat PEDOT:PSS samples. To minimize batch-to-batch variation, all cryo-EM measurements reported here were performed on a single batch (Batch# 9003838499, received on 07/2019). For measurements that required larger quantities of material (TGA and mechanical testing), we used a second PH1000 lot (Batch# 9008427769, received on 02/2022). To check that batch differences do not affect the main morphological conclusions, we also prepared films from both lots and imaged them by cryo-EM. As shown in Fig. S24, the resulting morphologies are similar in both cases, with fibrillar regions visible in each. No filtration was performed for liquid or solid sample processing. Unless otherwise mentioned, all other chemicals used in this study were purchased from Millipore Sigma. Stock solutions of Li-TFSI (Lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide and EMIM-TFSI (1-Ethyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide) were made in water with 320 mg/mL concentration. For PEDOT:PSS+salt samples, an appropriate amount of salt solution was added to the as-received PEDOT:PSS to achieve a dispersion with 60 wt% PEDOT:PSS solid content and 40 wt% salt content (assuming 1.2% solid content of as-received PEDOT:PSS solution). These dispersions were used without further purification. For PEDOT:PSS+EMIM-TFSI dispersions, the salt solution was added to the PEDOT:PSS dispersion in 10–20 µL portions to avoid strong aggregation of PEDOT:PSS upon the addition of EMIM-TFSI. All solutions, after being vortexed for 5 min, were stored in amber vials at room temperature before processing. PEDOT:PSS films were prepared by spin-coating solutions on pre-cleaned substrates with a 4000 revolutions per minute (rpm) spin speed. The coated substrates were further annealed at 125 °C for 10 min. Water-treated films were prepared by exposing the pre-annealed PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films to deionized water (DI water) for 60 s. These films were further spun at 4000 rpm to dry the films and were annealed at 125 °C for 10 min.

Cryo-EM sample preparation
2D micrographs of the solution were acquired using cryo-EM. Quantifoil Holey Carbon Grids, 300 mesh, with 1 μm hole size and 2 μm spacings (Quantifoil MicroTools, Jena, Germany) were used for the vitrification of neat PEDOT:PSS and additive-containing PEDOT:PSS solutions. A FEI Vitrobot (FEI Company, Hillsboro, OR) was used for the vitrification of PEDOT:PSS solutions. All solutions were kept at room temperature before plunge freezing in liquid ethane. The Vitrobot chamber was kept at 4 °C at 10% relative humidity (RH). 3.5 µL of the solution was administrated to the TEM grids for liquid cryo-EM sample preparation. The vitrification was done using filter papers mounted to the blotting pads with one or two cycles of blotting based on the viscosity of the samples. PEDOT:PSS+salt solutions usually possess a higher viscosity, which necessitates at least two cycles of blotting to achieve a thin enough specimen for TEM imaging. Blotting cycles each lasted for 3 s, with a total blotting time of 6 s for two cycles. The grids were quickly moved to liquid nitrogen containers after the initial vitrification. High-resolution cryo-EM imaging of liquid samples was performed on the FEI Talos Arctica (Thermo Fisher Scientific, OR, USA) at the Huck Institute of the Life Sciences at the Pennsylvania State University. The measurements were conducted using a 200 kV electron source and a Falcon 4 direct electron detector in counting mode. The nanoprobe mode of the microscope with a 70 μm C2 aperture, with a spot size of 5, was employed to collect the TEM micrographs. All cryo-EM micrographs were collected with an electron dose of <40 e/Å2. Magnifications of 73,000x, 92,000x, 120,000x, and 150,000x with the pixel sizes of 0.206 nm, 0.153 nm, 0.122 nm, and 0.0933 nm, respectively, were used for cryo-EM imaging of vitrified solutions. Binning of 1 (no camera pixel binning) was used for the images with 4096×4096 pixels. Binning of 2 was used for displaying of cryo-EM micrographs. Digital Micrograph software was used for Fast Fourier transform of cryo-EM micrographs. Fiji software was used for azimuthal integration of 2D FFT profiles. Additional PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI samples were prepared using the CryoSol VitroJet vitrification system operated at 4 °C and 100% RH. Samples were pin-printed onto Quantifoil grids (R2/1, 200 mesh) under the setting for medium ice thickness (Plasma cleaning, 60 s; Spacing, 90 μm; Standoff, 10 μm; Velocity, 1 mm/s; Pin dewpoint offset, 0.1 °C; Grid dewpoint offset, 0 °C; spiral pattern for deposition), followed by rapid vitrification with a liquid ethane jet. The controlled environment ensured reproducible film thickness and minimized sample evaporation prior to freezing.

Solid PEDOT:PSS thin films for cryo-EM and standard TEM measurements were prepared by spin coating of PEDOT:PSS dispersions on a silicon (Si) substrate with a sacrificial layer of PMMA. Silicon/PMMA samples were exposed to UV-Ozone for a 10 min duration to improve the surface energy of the PMMA layer. This leads to better wettability and coverage of PEDOT:PSS on PMMA. After thermal annealing at 125 °C, the Si/PMMA/PEDOT:PSS samples were scratched with metal tweezers and submerged in chlorobenzene. Due to the preferential solubility of PMMA in chlorobenzene, we achieved free-standing PEDOT:PSS thin films which were subsequently picked up by Lacey carbon TEM grids. In the next step, TEM grids were annealed at 90 °C for 10 min to ensure no residual solvents remained on the film.

Moisture-induced thin films were prepared by exposing solid films on TEM grids to either 30 or 100% RH in an FEI Vitrobot chamber before vitrification of the TEM grids with liquid ethane. The chamber temperature was kept at 25 °C before vitrification to limit the formation of frost on solid films during the vitrification process. TEM grids were stored at each humidity level for at least 20 min to ensure the proper swelling of the thin films. No blotting was employed before thin sample vitrification. TEM grids were stored in liquid nitrogen before clipping and loading in the autosampler.

Unless otherwise mentioned, cryo-EM micrographs of solid samples were collected on an FEI Titan Krios microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific, OR, USA) at the Huck Institute of the Life Sciences at the Pennsylvania State University. The measurements were conducted using a 300 kV electron source and a Falcon 4 direct electron detector in counting mode. The nanoprobe mode of the microscope with a 70 μm C2 aperture and a spot size of 5 was employed to collect TEM micrographs. All cryo-EM micrographs were collected with an electron dose of <50 e/Å2. High-resolution micrographs and low-resolution micrographs of solid thin films were collected at 150,000x (pixel size of 0.043 nm), and 47,000x magnifications (pixel size of 0.14 nm), respectively. At high magnification, the electron dose rate was set to be less than 30 e/Å2 s. Binning of 1 (no camera pixel binning) was used for the imaging with 4096×4096 pixels. Binning of 2 and 4 were used for displaying of micrographs imaged at 47,000x and 150,000x, respectively.

For cryo-EM of solutions, we use 4 °C with 100% RH to suppress evaporation in the blot-to-plunge interval and to promote formation of uniform vitreous ice. In contrast, for hydrated solid films, cooling the chamber (and therefore the Cu grid) below ambient temperature can lead to water condensation on the film. Upon plunging, these water droplets can convert to crystalline ice, and affect the film morphology and TEM imaging. To avoid condensation while maintaining hydration, we therefore set the chamber to 25 °C for solid films. The differences between Fig. 2b/2d and Fig. 3a/3b arise mainly from imaging magnification. Figure 3a–b were recorded at higher magnification (150,000x) than Fig. 2 (47,000x), giving a smaller pixel size and better sampling of high spatial frequencies; as a result, lattice planes are resolved more clearly. In contrast, the lower-magnification images provide a larger field of view and stronger low-frequency contrast, so micelles and lamellar spacing can be visualized in the same frame. To extract defocus values for both solid and solution cryo-EM micrographs, we used the EMAN2 software package. EMAN2 estimates the defocus values by analyzing the contrast transfer function (CTF) patterns in the Fourier transform (FFT) of micrographs and is more accurate than readings from the microscope that rely on establishing the eucentric height60. In EMAN2 CTF fitting, all parameters were left at their default values except pixel size, accelerating voltage (kV), and spherical aberration (Cs, mm). Cs was set to 0.01 mm for the Krios and 2.7 mm for the Arctica.

STEM-EELS
Standard STEM-EELS results were acquired using a Talos F200X (Thermo Fisher Scientific, OR, USA) at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV equipped with a Gatan Imaging Filter (GIF). EELS results were collected with 0.3 eV/channel dispersion, 16 µs pixel time, and 30 nm step size. Auto zero loss peak detection and auto-focus were performed prior to the data collection. Cryo-STEM-EELS measurements were performed on a FEI Titan Krios microscope equipped with a Gatan energy filter and K2 camera. The micro-probe mode was used for Cryo-STEM-EELS to reduce the local temperature increase during EELS data collection. Cryo-STEM-EELS results were collected using a high signal-to-noise ratio (Hi-SNR) aperture with 0.5 eV/channel dispersion, 15 nm pixel size, and 5 s pixel time with the EELS exposure time of 0.1 s at 130 eV (high loss).

Grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering
For grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS), samples were spin coated on pre-cleaned bare Si substrates at 4000 rpm. GIWAXS was conducted at beamline 7.3.3, Advanced Light Source, Lawerence Berkeley National Laboratory61. X-ray energy, beam current, and sample-detector distance were 10 keV, 500 mA, and 281 mm. AgB was used to calibrate the Pilatus 2M detector. GIWAXS scans of samples were measured at 0.12, 0.14, and 0.16° incidence angle for an exposure time of 10 s. In-plane and out-of-plane sector cuts of 2D scattering images ranged 18° from 0° to 90°, respectively. XI-CAM was used to reduce 2D scattering images to 1D sector cuts62.

Small-angle X-ray scattering
SAXS measurements were conducted at beamline 7.3.3, Advanced Light Source, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory62. A 10 keV X-ray beam was used to probe the sample at 0°. A Pilatus 2M detector collected 2D scattering data at a distance 3.5 m away from the sample. 2D scattering images were reduced to 1D profiles using Nika on Igor Pro63. For film samples, films were cast onto 100 nm thick silicon nitride windows (Norcada NX5100C). The drop cast films were left at room temperature overnight to dry. In the next step, the silicon nitride coated samples were annealed at 120 °C for 30 min to remove water residual. Film samples were loaded into a 3D-printed humidity chamber with Kapton windows. Humid air from a LINKAM RH95 humidity controller flowed into the chamber at controlled flow rates to keep the environment static at 40% and 85% RH. SAXS of a blank silicon nitride window was used for background subtraction for each RH. 120-second exposure times were used.

Conductivity
A Micromanipulator Co. 2800 manual probe station and Keithley 4200 SCS Parameter Analyzer were used to conduct independent four-point probe measurements inside an anhydrous, N2 glovebox. Probes were 44-6000-S-NA Probe Holder with Integrated Tip from Micromanipulator Co. Voltage drop was measured while sweeping current for four-point probe measurements, where the Au electrode distance was 100 μm. Resistances were extracted from the slopes of independent sweeps, and film thicknesses measured via profilometry were used to calculate conductivities. Conductivities were averaged from 9, 6, and 16 independent electrode sets for neat PEDOT:PSS, PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI, and PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI-w, respectively. Au electrode dimensions for four-point probe measurements were 220 μm wide, 100 μm long, and 100 nm thick.

GRATEv2 analysis
We employed the open-source GRATEv2 (Graph-based Analysis of TEM) framework to identify and characterize crystalline domains in the HRTEM images of our polymeric samples. In brief, GRATEv2 executes a parameterized image-processing pipeline that involves (1) morphological operations (e.g., blurring, thresholding, opening and closing), (2) skeletonizing line-like image features, and (3) constructing a graph representation to cluster those skeletal elements into distinct crystalline regions. This approach is particularly effective for complex polymer morphologies, as it robustly separates overlapping or coalesced crystal domains while preserving critical features such as boundaries and orientation angles. Following detection, GRATEv2 also extracts essential microstructural metrics (e.g., crystal area, orientation, aspect ratios, and d-spacing), enabling quantitative comparisons across different samples.

For our dataset, the employed parameters are shown in Table 1 for the GRATEv2 pipeline. These parameters were chosen to balance sensitivity to faint or irregular crystal edges with robustness against small artifacts. The GRATEv2 output includes a segmentation mask of the detected crystals, as well as a table of individual crystal properties (e.g., d-spacing and orientation), providing a comprehensive view of each sample’s microstructure for subsequent analyses.

Crack onset strain
Polystyrene-block-poly(ethylene-ran-butylene)-block-polystyrene (SEBS) was used as a supporting stretchable layer for crack onset strain measurements. SEBS (Millipore Sigma) was dissolved in toluene with 120 mg/mL concentration. The SEBS films were fabricated by drop casting solution in a 7.5 × 7.5 cm2 mold. The drop cast SEBS solution was left at room temperature overnight and subsequently annealed at 60 °C for 1 h. In the next step 30 mL of neat PEDOT:PSS or PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI solution was drop cast on the SEBS layer. The SEBS/PEDOT:PSS or SEBS/PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI films were kept at room temperature overnight. This step is crucial in achieving a uniform PEDOT:PSS film on the SEBS layer. After the evaporation of the majority of the water content of PEDOT:PSS films, the films were annealed at 60 °C for 1 hour. The SEBS/PEDOT:PSS films were cut into 1 × 4 cm2 samples for crack onset strain measurements (COS). COS measurements were performed using the manual custom-built stretching stage. 0 % RH measurements were performed inside a nitrogen filled glovebox after annealing PEDOT:PSS or PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI samples at 80 °C for 1 hour. This annealing step ensures that residual moisture in PEDOT:PSS samples is removed before acquiring COS results. A minimum of three samples were tested for each doping and humidity condition.

The manuscript by Ghasemi and co-authors presents a thorough cryo-EM structural analyses of PEDOT:PSS in solution and in the solid state with and without secondary dopants.

### Reviewer 2

Ghasemi et al report on their characterization of different PEDOT:PSS formulation both in the solution and thin film using electron microscopy. The authors show the hierarchical structure of PEDOT:PSS, with micelles, nanofibers, and semicrystalline and disordered regions. I find the work very exciting. It is incredible to clearly see structural features in the solutions and films that normally must be inferred from indirect measurements. This methodology is certainly the future of polymer microstructural characterization, and I expect this work will be important in the field.
However, the conclusions drawn from the analysis of the images are not entirely clear, and there are questions about the sample preparation and the assumptions made when classifying the features seen in TEM. For this reason, I recommend a revision prior to accepting into Nature Communications. My specific comments are below.
First, the paper needs to explain what exactly is being imaged for the vitrified PEDOT:PSS dispersions. Presumably during blotting, some of the water is absorbed into the paper, concentrating PEDOT:PSS in the dispersion. This likely drives the aggregation into fibril structures that is observed. How representative are these images of the dispersion itself? Is there any evidence for fibers forming in the as is dispersion before the blotting process? And how does the aggregation of PEDOT:PSS micelles during blotting relate to aggregation during other common processing methods (spin-coating, blade-coating, dropcasting, etc.)?
It doesn’t appear that there is much variation in particle size within a sample, why is that? DLS characterization of particle sizes in PEDOT:PSS dispersions have shown a wide dispersity [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcis.2020.09.070].
I’m a little confused about the proposed structure in Fig 1c. The cartoons show a micelle with a lot of messy, tangled polymer, with a PEDOT rich core and PSS rich shell. However, the size of the micelle in the images is 2.7 nm up to 4.7 nm, is on the order of 2-3x the PEDOT:PSS lamellar spacing distance when the molecules are tightly packed. How would all of that polymer fit into such a small volume, especially when it isn’t tightly packed? In panel j, the micelle diameter is smaller than two repeated lamellae of the shell of the nanofiber. Is this picture physically feasible?
Also, in the cartoons, why are the PEDOT chains drawn as very short segments in the neat film, but very long (spanning several micelles) in the secondary doping case? Shouldn’t the Mw of PEDOT:PSS be constant? What is the image intended to convey?
In the FFT insets in Fig 3a and Fig S3, there are several rings all the way out to ~3 nm-1. It is surprising to see so many strong peaks since the GIWAXS ~4 peaks which are fairly weak. What is the physical origin of these rings in the FFT images?
Why do the HRTEM images in Fig 3 look so different from images in Fig 2b and 2c? Is the imaging mode different? The scale of the images in Fig 3 appear to be similar to the insets Fig 2. Does this mean some of the contrast in the low-res images is due to imaging artefacts?
While the paper shows several interesting modalities for cryo-EM characterization, there is very little continuity in the sample choice. First, 4 different secondary dopants are investigated for solution imaging, but only two of the four are measured as solid films. The authors then show humidity dependent crystal size but only apply the analysis to one formulation (Li-TFSI secondary dopant) and compare the results to GISAX measured at two different humidities from the TEM experiment humidities. Finally, they show SETM-EELS to explore where moisture is located within solid films, but the sample changes again and the authors introduce PEDOT:PSS + Li-TFSI with salt-removed. A clear demonstration of how these techniques complement one another and can be combined to build up a holistic microstructural picture for a single materials system would be much more convincing than the current variety of samples explored here. I was also surprised that the PEGDA doped PEDOT:PSS was not included in the mechanical analysis since the authors discussed in the introduction that PEGDA is usually added to improve stretchability.

## Paper

## Abstract

Soft and conducting organic materials are ideal candidates for stretchable bioelectronics and wearable devices. Despite recent advances, our understanding of conducting polymer nanostructures and how they arise remains incomplete, given the limited high-resolution studies and molecular-level descriptions of these systems. Here, we employ cryogenic transmission electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to investigate the evolution of poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrenesulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) morphology in solution and the resulting solid state structure in the presence of ionic and molecular additives. Our results reveal the formation of heterostructural elongated fibers consisting of PEDOT:PSS micelles in solution. Cryo-EM further reveals that additives increase the number of fibrils, in addition to inducing the formation of crystalline domains. We observe that fibril and crystalline phases in solutions act as a template for the growth of these nanostructures in the solid state. Furthermore, exploiting cryo-EM reveals the role of solid-liquid interactions in PEDOT:PSS through the imaging of PEDOT:PSS nanostructures after the hydration of thin films. Hydration leads to the swelling of heterostructural fibers while reducing the crystalline domain size. Such behavior explains the mechanical robustness of PEDOT:PSS thin films processed with various additives as well as the high electrical conductivity of PEDOT:PSS in applications such as organic electorchemical transistors.

## Introduction

Mixed ionic-electronic conductors have attracted tremendous attention due to their unique properties and applicability in a wider range of devices, such as batteries1, fuel cells2, and organic electrochemical transistors3,4. Organic mixed-ionic electronic conductors, particularly conjugated polymeric systems, have opened new prospects in applications in biosensing5 and neuromorphic computing6. Poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrenesulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) is one of the most widely used polymeric mixed ionic-electronic conductors due to its commercial availability, high electrical/ionic conductivity7,8, and mechanical compliance7,9. This prototypical mixed conductor relies on a mixture of conjugated and ionic polymers, although how interactions between the two components, processing, and additives govern assembly, microstructure and macroscopic properties remain an open question.

PEDOT:PSS in its pristine form possesses a low electrical conductivity, near 1 S/cm3,7,10,11. The addition of high boiling point solvents11, “secondary dopants” such as ionic liquids and salts12,13, and post-deposition acid treatment14 can substantially enhance electrical conductivity by three orders of magnitude over their pristine counterparts. In addition to the significant boost to conductivity, ionic and molecular additives have also been linked to an increase in the stretchability and flexibility of PEDOT:PSS, a key property for fabricating wearable electronics7,12,13.

A large body of work has focused on studying structure-function relationships in PEDOT:PSS under different processing conditions7,12,13,15–19. Despite these efforts, a holistic picture describing the PEDOT:PSS morphology remains elusive, in part due to morphological complexities and the lack of real space imaging techniques conveying the solution and solid-state properties. For instance, we commonly accept that PEDOT:PSS microstructure consists of core-shell micelles with PEDOT-rich cores and PSS-rich coronas. Despite this common assumption, the reported core-shell size extracted from neutron, X-ray, and light scattering techniques ranges from a few nanometers15 to hundreds of nanometers20,21. The role of additives further complicates the morphological picture3. X-ray and neutron scattering measurements point to the formation of rod-like structures21 in PEDOT:PSS with added salts, as well as an increase in the degree of crystallinity7 of PEDOT:PSS through the breakdown of core-shell and phase segregation of PEDOT and PSS. Nevertheless, important aspects of the PEDOT:PSS morphology remain unresolved, such as the size and distribution of crystalline domains and the correlation between rod-like aggregates and crystalline phases. Despite the partial success of the core-shell breakdown model, this description fails to explain multiple PEDOT:PSS properties, such as the simultaneous increase in electrical conductivity and increase in mechanical compliance, in particular of modern formulations of PEDOT:PSS7,22. This behavior is in contrast with other conjugated polymer systems, where a trade-off exists between charge transport (and crystallinity) and mechanical compliance23,24. We propose that the lack of a comprehensive morphological model predicting the physical properties of PEDOT:PSS mainly stems from reliance on scattering and spectroscopy techniques to characterize the complex global and local morphology of PEDOT:PSS.

Here, we reveal how the microstructure impacts the mechanical and electrical properties of PEDOT:PSS using a combination of cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS), and X-ray scattering. Exploiting high-resolution cryo-EM reveals the nanostructure evolution of PEDOT:PSS dispersions upon the addition of ionic and nonionic additives. We used bis(trifluoromethane)sulfonimide lithium (Li-TFSI) and 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide (EMIM-TFSI) salts due to their strong cation exchange capability with PEDOT:PSS22. Polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) was selected as a nonionic additive because it can enable highly-conductive, stretchable PEDOT:PSS-based bioelectronics9,10. Our results reveal that ionic and PEGDA additives lead to the formation of elongated fibers and chain packing in solutions. Further analysis of cryo-EM results reveals that elongated fibers form through the coalescence and self-assembly of PEDOT:PSS micelles that often exhibit an outer layer of extended and stacked chains. The presence of these heterostructural fibers has direct implications on the mechanical and electrical properties of PEDOT:PSS.

High-resolution cryo-EM imaging of solid films, which are processed from PEDOT:PSS solutions with the various additives, confirms the formation and growth of crystalline domains and heterostructural fibers in solid samples. Furthermore, by employing a combination of cryo-EM, EELS, and an automated crystal feature extraction framework (called Graph based Analysis of Transmission Electron Microscopy, GRATEv225), we show how exposure to moisture reorganizes the PEDOT:PSS nanostructure leading to smaller crystalline domains while heterostructural fibers swell. The former observation is consistent with the reduction in electrical conductivity of PEDOT:PSS in the presence of moisture26,27, while the latter explains the complex mechanical properties of PEDOT:PSS with ionic and PEGDA additives. Our results also show that additives can enhance the hydrophilicity of PEDOT:PSS, leading to higher moisture absorbance and resulting in higher mechanical compliance and a larger crack onset strain in these samples. Subsequently, the combination of heterostructural fibers swelling and reorganization of crystalline domains leads to the formation of simultaneously conductive and stretchable PEDOT:PSS thin films. Our work provides a framework for the complex interplay between morphological, mechanical, and electrical properties of modern formulations of PEDOT:PSS used in different applications, such as implant electrodes5, wearable electronics9, and organic electrochemical transistors8,28.

## Results

Cryo-EM of PEDOT:PSS dispersions
Beam damage is one of the main factors limiting the resolution and detailed analysis of organic structures in real space. Cryo-EM has been extensively used in the study of biological samples29,30 to both minimize electron beam damage31–33 and enable studies of hydrated (vitrified) samples31–33. We used cryo-EM to track PEDOT:PSS self-assembly with salt additives. Previously, we showed that the addition of ionic species lead to the formation and self-assembly of elongated fibers in the solution phase of PEDOT:PSS3. Other recent studies have also reported elongated fibrils in doped PEDOT:PSS17,34,35. Despite these initial observations, the lack of high-resolution structural imaging of PEDOT:PSS in either solution or solid films precludes a complete description of PEDOT:PSS phase formation and microstructure. Specifically, the distribution of crystalline domains and the inner structure of elongated fibers in highly conductive and stretchable PEDOT:PSS remain underexplored.

Solution cryo-EM measurements were performed on vitrified PEDOT:PSS samples at liquid nitrogen temperature (see the Methods section for details). Figure 1a–b shows a schematic of the plunge freezing of TEM grids and the chemical structure of PEDOT:PSS and ionic and PEGDA additives, respectively. Schematics of PEDOT:PSS dispersions containing isolated micelles and aggregated micelles in heterostructural fibers are shown in Fig. 1c–d, respectively. High-resolution cryo-EM shows the presence of two distinct domains in neat PEDOT:PSS solutions, (i) isolated micelles with a size of 4.1 ± 1.3 nm, and (ii) elongated fibers (Fig. 1e–g). On the other hand, PEDOT:PSS solutions containing ionic and PEGDA additives, in addition to the higher density of elongated fibers, also show lattice planes of PEDOT:PSS in solution (Fig. 1h–p).

Previous work has used X-ray scattering measurements to propose that PEDOT:PSS micelles consist of a PEDOT-rich nanocrystalline core and a PSS-rich corona15. The higher mass density of the crystalline PEDOT-rich core when compared to the amorphous PSS-rich corona leads us to assume that electron scattering from the micelles is dominated by the core region. As a result, we associate the ca. 3–4 nm features in cryo-EM micrographs with the PEDOT-rich core of PEDOT:PSS micelles. At this point, the size of the PSS-rich corona region cannot be independently extracted from cryo-EM, mainly due to the small scattering contrast between solvated PSS-rich regions and water.

A comparison of micelle sizes in solutions reveals that ionic additives decrease the diameter of PEDOT-rich cores (3.1 ± 0.5 nm), while solutions with PEGDA exhibit micelle sizes comparable to those of neat PEDOT:PSS (3.9 ± 0.8 nm) (see Figs. S1–S2). A reduction in micelle size upon the addition of salts to PEDOT:PSS has been previously reported, which has been attributed to the screening of interchain charge repulsion15,36. Previously reported micelle sizes extracted from solutions of PEDOT:PSS using measurements of the hydrodynamic radius obtained from dynamic light scattering (DLS) show a dominant size distribution between 3 to 15 nm and a few micelles up to 30 nm37. As shown in Fig. 1, we also observe smaller micelles and larger aggregate structures. In addition, given that solvated PSS chains are likely not visible in cryo-EM, we expect micelles in our micrographs to appear smaller than values reported from DLS or SAXS. The micelle size apparent from our cryo-EM images and previous work37 suggests that PEDOT exists as oligomers with limited chain lengths.

We attribute the chain stacking with 1.4–1.6 nm spacing, observed in solution cryo-EM micrographs, to PEDOT:PSS lamella stacks that have previously been attributed to the presence of alternating PEDOT and PSS chains3,38. Examples of these lamellae lattice fringes (parallel lines in cryo-EM micrographs) are indicated by the orange arrows in Fig. 1i–o. To rule out Fresnel-fringe or defocus artifacts, we measured the lamellar spacing at multiple defocus settings; the spacing (~1.5 nm) remained invariant with defocus (Figs. S3–S4). As mentioned before, cryo-EM micrographs reveal fibers with a complex heterostructure of coalesced polymer micelles and extended stacked chains that we attribute to a crystalline, or “proto-crystalline” phase. Figure 1h–j shows that these heterostructural fibers consist of small micelles (core of about 3 nm) surrounded by a crystalline phase parallel to the long axis of the fibers.

As shown in Fig. S5, and consistent with the Vitrobot-prepared (“blot-based”) micrographs in Fig. 1, samples prepared with Vitroject (non-contact, jet-based)39 also display clear elongated fibers in PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI dispersions. The agreement between blot-based and non-contact preparation highlights that these fibers are intrinsic to the PEDOT:PSS formulations, not artifacts of the blotting process. Furthermore, these heterostructural fibers can also be observed in PEDOT:PSS+EMIM-TFSI and PEDOT:PSS+PEGDA solution mixtures (Fig. 1k–m, n–p). Additional examples of micrographs collected at different defocus settings and micrographs highlighting lamella stacks plus micelles in PEDOT:PSS dispersions are shown in Figs. S6 and S7. We observe that increasing the self-assembly time after adding the additives leads to more elongated fibers and fewer isolated micelles in PEDOT:PSS+EMIM-TFSI dispersions (Fig. S8). This rise in fiber density with time, together with the drop in isolated micelles, is consistent with our prior results3 and points to micelle coalescence driving the formation of elongated fibers. As will be discussed in the following sections, the presence of crystalline phases and heterostructural fibers has a significant effect on the physical and electrical properties of PEDOT:PSS thin films.

Given the similar trends across various PEDOT:PSS systems, subsequent sections center on PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI as a model system to examine morphological evolution of PEDOT:PSS processed with additives.

Cryo-EM of solid films
To elucidate how films assemble from PEDOT:PSS solutions, we performed cryo-EM on spin-coated thin films of PEDOT:PSS processed with and without additives. At lower magnifications, neat PEDOT:PSS films (Fig. S9) show a uniform morphology, while magnified micrographs also show the presence of both PEDOT:PSS lamella stacks and micelles. The crystalline domains in neat PEDOT:PSS are generally around 10-15 nm long and <5 nm wide. The PEDOT-rich cores of the micelles in neat PEDOT:PSS films have an oval shape with a long axis of ~3.5 nm. Unlike in neat PEDOT:PSS solutions, elongated fibers are not visible in cryo-EM micrographs of solid PEDOT:PSS films. We speculate that fibers in neat PEDOT:PSS strongly coalesce or breakdown, making them challenging to identify in micrographs. On the other hand, PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI (see Fig. 2a) and PEDOT:PSS+PEGDA (see Fig. S10) samples show a significantly more heterogeneous structure than neat PEDOT:PSS. This is in line with the presence of more fibers and crystalline domains in solutions of additive-containing PEDOT:PSS formulations. Similarly to the aggregates visible in solution, high magnification of the structure reveals that elongated fibers in PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films appear to form through the coalescence of polymer micelles (Fig. 2b). Indeed, lamellar structures are now apparent throughout the film and are not limited to areas surrounding micellar fibers.

Overall, we see a close resemblance between solution and solid domains in PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI, with larger crystalline domains (>20 nm thick crystals) observed in the solid samples. Thus, the heterostructural fibers and crystalline domains in solution template the growth of the subsequent structures in solid thin films. We also see a fibril structure in samples containing ethylene glycol as a solvent additive and (3-glycidyloxypropyl)trimethoxysilane (GOPS) cross-linker (Fig. S12). PEDOT:PSS+ethylene glycol+GOPS is perhaps the most common formulation used in organic electrochemical transistor devices. Further analysis of cryo-EM micrographs using frequency cut-off filters (see Fig. S13) reveals that the crystalline domains in PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI do not align with the orientation of heterostructured fibers. Therefore, although large fibrils in PEDOT:PSS are assumed to be composed of PEDOT (or PEDOT-rich) crystals11,13,17, our work clearly shows that micelles, likely composed of PEDOT and PSS mixtures, make up these domains. We speculate that this structure, with PEDOT proto-crystals coating the outside of micellar structures, is crucial for establishing highly conducting phases by precluding the need to disrupt an insulating PSS corona that was previously assumed to be present.

Besides the PEDOT:PSS lamellar phase with 1.4–1.6 nm spacing (which could correspond to the PEDOT:PSS (100) crystal planes)40, cryo-EM also captures domains with a lattice spacing of ~0.7 nm. The latter spacing corresponds to the pure PEDOT lamella stacking (see Fig. S14 for cryo-EM micrograph and subsequent FFT of the crystalline domains with ~0.7 nm spacing). Compared to in solution, lamella stacks spacings appear to be slightly larger in solid samples. To further investigate PEDOT:PSS microstructure, we performed grazing incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) measurements on PEDOT:PSS samples with and without additives. Figures 2e and S11 show 1D GIWAXS profiles along the in-plane and out-of-plane orientations, respectively, for neat PEDOT:PSS and PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films. Figure S11 further shows GIWAXS profiles of additional PEDOT:PSS thin films processed with additives. Previous work has associated the peaks at 0.39 Å−1 (16.1 Å) and 0.28 Å−1 (22.5 Å) with stacking of two different variations of alternating PEDOT and PSS chains18,38,41 (as shown in Fig. S15 and Table S1). The peaks at 0.89 Å−1 (7.1 Å), 1.27 Å−1 (4.9 Å), and 1.8 Å−1 (3.5 Å) are associated with the neat PEDOT lamella stacking7, PSS chain stacking18, and PEDOT π-π stacking, respectively18.

The reported diffraction peak positions and spacings can vary slightly depending on the type of additive and measurement conditions, such as humidity18,42. Because lattice fringes are visible only when the electron beam is approximately parallel to those lattice planes, periodicities oriented out-of-plane, which project along the beam, are not visible in TEM micrographs. Thus, the spacings apparent in in-plane GIWAXS (lamella stacks with 15–16 Å spacing) correspond to visible chain stacking in TEM micrographs. Overall, the combination of solution and solid film cryo-EM provides an opportunity to identify key features of the microstructure and how they evolve from solution to film.

Solid-liquid Interactions
We expect different responses from crystalline domains and heterostructural fibers when exposed to moisture. To investigate this hypothesis, we exposed PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films to moisture (100% relative humidity (RH)) before plunge-freezing the samples with liquid ethane (see Methods section for further details). This approach allows us to monitor the morphological evolution in high-conductivity PEDOT:PSS thin films in the presence of water.

As shown in cryo-EM images in Fig. 2c, upon exposure to moisture, PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films show a uniform morphology with some inhomogeneity observed in the density of PEDOT:PSS micelles. We also show HRTEM images of PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI recorded at 30% and 100% relative humidity under varying defocus conditions in Fig. S16. Moisture exposure improves the contrast of polymer micelles, as can be seen in Fig. 2d. Given the expected thickness increase of PEDOT:PSS films upon hydration42,43, the improvement in scattering contrast cannot be explained by reduced inelastic electron scattering or a reduced number of overlapping features in hydrated samples. Subsequently, we deduce that upon exposure to moisture, the PSS-rich shell of the micelles swells, decreasing the scattering from the shell and improving the contrast between the PEDOT-rich core and the swollen PSS-rich corona. This shows that heterostructural fibers consist of self-assembled core-shell PEDOT:PSS micelles that swell upon exposure to water. Figure 2f shows the 1D small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) SAXS profiles of drop cast neat PEDOT:PSS and PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI at two different RH levels. While the SAXS profiles from neat PEDOT:PSS show minimal differences between 40% and 85% RH, PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI samples show a clear change that corresponds to the formation of mesoscale structures upon exposure to higher moisture.

The limited field of view of high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) images often limits analyses to qualitative changes. Automated sampling and large-quantity data collection, developed for the study of biological samples44–47, may promote the extraction of quantitative microstructural information from HRTEM. This approach remains under-explored for the quantitative analysis of the morphology of conjugated polymers. Recently, Gamdha et al.25 developed software for a Graph based Analysis of Transmission Electron Microscopy (GRATEv2) of polymeric samples25,48, which can identify crystalline domains from images at high speed, providing information on domain size, orientation, and area.

We employed GRATEv2 to analyze crystalline domain size and distribution in PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films before and after hydration (exposure to 100% RH). HRTEM micrographs of PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films at 30% and 100% RH can be seen in Fig. 3a–b, respectively. Figure 3c shows the flow chart of the GRATEv2 analysis. Figure 3d–e shows the subsequent GRATEv2 output figures of micrographs presented in Fig. 3a–b, respectively. The crystalline domains with a lattice spacing of ~1.5-16 nm ((100) PEDOT:PSS lamella spacing) are shown with the purple regions. Additional cryo-EM examples at 30% and 100% RH, together with their GRATEv2 analyses, are shown in Figure S17. A histogram of crystalline domain sizes is presented in Fig. 3f. HRTEM shows that hydration leads to the formation of smaller crystalline domains in PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI with an average domain area of 117 nm2 at 30% RH versus 74 nm2 at 100% RH. These results show that crystalline domains respond differently to water absorption compared to heterostructural fibers. While crystalline domains shrink in size, heterostructural fibers swell significantly upon hydration. The distinct difference in microstructural evolution of crystalline domains and heterostructural fibers upon hydration shows that these two domains possess different nanostructures. As will be discussed in the next section, the direct imaging of nanocrystalline domains and heterostructural fibers allows us to explain the mechanical and electrical properties of PEDOT:PSS upon exposure to humidity and moisture.

Electrical and mechanical properties of PEDOT:PSS
The high electrical conductivity and mechanical compliance of PEDOT:PSS, often achieved by the addition of ionic additives, are the main factors driving the widespread use of this mixed ionic-electronic polymer in various applications3,7,9,49. In this section, we explore the correlation between morphology, conductivity, and mechanical properties of PEDOT:PSS in the presence of ionic additives. Consistent with prior studies7,12,13,22, we observe an increase in the electrical conductivity of PEDOT:PSS thin films by two to three orders of magnitude following film processing using ionic additives and water treatment of salt-containing films (Fig. S18). The significant increase in electrical conductivity of PEDOT:PSS is often closely correlated with an increase in crystallinity of PEDOT:PSS processed with different additives7,12,13. This is consistent with the larger number of crystalline domains observed in cryo-EM of PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films (See Fig. 3d).

Compared to the mechanisms behind the enhancement of electrical conductivity, the improvement in mechanical properties of PEDOT:PSS in the presence of ionic additives is less understood. To ascertain the role of structure on mechanical properties in PEDOT:PSS, we performed crack onset strain (COS) measurements of neat PEDOT:PSS and PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI at two different humidity levels (See Methods section for more details). At 70% RH, cracks appear in neat PEDOT:PSS and PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI at 11±5 % and 27±8 % strains, respectively (see Fig. 4a). On the other hand, when the same measurements were performed in a 0% RH glovebox, both neat PEDOT:PSS and the additive-loaded samples cracked at much lower strains (~2% COS), with dry PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI showing even slightly less stretchability compared to neat PEDOT:PSS. Upon hydration, a similar increasing trend in COS is also observed in PEDOT:PSS+PEGDA (Fig. S19). These results indicate that moisture uptake plays a substantial role in the mechanical properties of PEDOT:PSS processed with additives, including salts50.

To further investigate the effect of ionic additives and their subsequent removal upon water treatment, we performed thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) on neat PEDOT:PSS and PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI; results are shown in Fig. 4b. Neat PEDOT:PSS show two main mass loss transitions: the first transition completes around 100 °C; this transition is due to the evaporation of moisture within the PEDOT:PSS structure. The second transition at ~275 °C is associated with the chemical degradation of PEDOT:PSS. On the other hand, PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI shows a significantly different TGA profile. TGA from PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI does not show clear thermal transitions, but instead a continuous loss of sample mass, with an overall larger mass loss percentage compared to neat PEDOT:PSS. After water treatment (removing added salts), the thermogram reverts to the two-step profile for neat PEDOT:PSS, confirming that water absorption due to Li-TFSI is responsible for the broadened, continuous loss of sample mass (Fig. S20). The water uptake of films containing Li-TFSI likely leads to the formation of water-salt complexes within the PEDOT:PSS structure51,52.

We also measured the water uptake due to Li-TFSI using scanning transmission electron microscopy-electron energy loss spectroscopy (STEM-EELS) at room temperature and cryogenic conditions (Fig. S21). STEM-EELS allows us to establish a compositional-morphological relationship in PEDOT:PSS thin films processed with hydrophilic additives. Although ionic additives are linked to the improved stretchability of PEDOT:PSS, upon water treatment, the stretchability of PEDOT:PSS films significantly drops due to the removal of these additives13. We associate this behavior with the formation of water-salt complexes in PEDOT:PSS and subsequent elimination of these complexes after water treatment. This is consistent with the increase in oxygen composition (as an indicator for water absorption) when we compare PEDOT:PSS+Li-TFSI thin films before and after salt removal (Fig. 4c and Fig. S22).
